what: A hybrid app ships your web app inside a native shell: Capacitor hosts it in the phone's WebView and gives it native features through plugins, while Ionic supplies mobile-style UI components. One codebase reaches iOS, Android and the web.
like: Like a picture frame: the picture is your web app, and the frame (Capacitor) lets it hang on the phone's wall and use the doorbell, camera and storage.
why: One Angular codebase for web, iOS and Android
Native features such as camera or push through plugins
Ships through the app stores and can still be updated over the air

steps.d: You write Angular with Ionic components and build normal web assets.
Capacitor is a native runtime that runs those assets in the system WebView on iOS and Android.
Capacitor's Plugin API (Swift for iOS, Java for Android, JavaScript for web) exposes device features to your JS.
A WebView on a cheap phone is slow: keep JS small, defer heavy code, virtualise long lists, and avoid big DOM trees.
ion-virtual-scroll was removed in Ionic 7; use Angular CDK cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport inside ion-content.
Release through the stores; web-only fixes can follow through live updates.

numbers.l: minimum OS versions for the current Capacitor release
compressed JS budget to load in 3 s on a mid-range phone at P75 for JS-heavy apps (650 KiB at 5 s)
docs example itemSize, minBufferPx and maxBufferPx for CDK virtual scroll in Ionic

choices.t: Hybrid or native or cross-platform native
choices.d: Hybrid reuses web skills and one codebase; truly native gives best performance and platform feel; choose by team skills and performance needs.
Capacitor is the modern native container that keeps close to web standards; Cordova is the older alternative.
Set a JS budget from the slowest target phone, lazy-load routes and use @defer, virtualise lists, and test on a real low-end Android device.
If a plugin does not exist, write a small custom plugin or use the native SDK; keep the bridge calls coarse.

instead.why: A web-only install route when you do not need store distribution or native plugins
The general idea behind long lists on slow phones

breaks.d: Large JS bundle and large DOM in an old WebView.
breaks.see: Slow start, laggy scroll and taps
breaks.fix: Budget JS, lazy-load, virtual scroll, test on a low-end device

breaks.d: Many small plugin calls in a loop.
breaks.fix: Batch work into fewer, coarser native calls

breaks.d: App minimum OS below what Capacitor supports.
breaks.see: Build or runtime failures on old devices
breaks.fix: Set the app minimum to the Capacitor minimum (iOS 15.0, Android API 24)

say: I use Angular with Ionic components in a Capacitor shell, so one codebase ships to iOS, Android and web, with native features through plugins.
On low-end Android I treat the WebView as the bottleneck: a JS budget, lazy loading with @defer, CDK virtual scroll for lists, and testing on a real cheap phone.
Web-only fixes go out through live updates, native changes through the stores.

followups.a: Hybrid gives one codebase and web skills; if the product needs heavy animation or deep platform features, native or a native-rendering framework fits better.

followups.q: How do you keep long lists smooth?
followups.a: Use CDK virtual scroll inside ion-content so only the visible rows exist in the DOM, with fixed item sizes.

today: Capacitor is on v8 with iOS 15 and Android 7 as minimums, and Ionic points list virtualisation to the Angular CDK since ion-virtual-scroll was removed.

check.a: Runs your web app in a native WebView and exposes device features via plugins
d: Renders UI with native widgets only
check.why: It is a native container and runtime for web apps.
ion-virtual-scroll was removed in Ionic 7; the docs recommend the CDK.

check.q: Main performance risk on cheap Android hybrid apps?
check.a: Too much JavaScript and DOM in the WebView
check.why: A slow device plus a big bundle means slow start and scroll.
